claims.text: A quenching and partitioning heat treatment with carefully controlled temperatures can simultaneously increase strength and ductility.
Quenching and partitioning stabilizes retained austenite.
The initial material is a fully austenitized medium-carbon steel.
The Q&P procedure quenches the steel to a temperature between Ms and Mf before elevating it to a partitioning temperature.
A partitioning temperature in the range of 200–400 °C can be used.
The treatment produces stabilized retained austenite within a predominantly martensitic matrix.
Retained austenite undergoes strain-induced transformation during deformation.
Strain-induced transformation of retained austenite provides additional plasticity.
Strain-induced transformation of retained austenite enhances fracture resistance.
A predominantly martensitic matrix maintains high strength while retained austenite contributes plasticity.
The Q&P-treated steel will have higher strength than the same steel after conventional quenching and tempering.
The Q&P-treated steel will have greater ductility than the same steel after conventional quenching and tempering.
Q&P effectiveness varies with steel composition, austenitizing conditions, and quenching and partitioning parameters.
Over-partitioning or under-partitioning can reduce the retained-austenite fraction.
A reduced retained-austenite fraction can diminish the proposed mechanical-property gains.
The partitioning temperature and duration required to maximize retained-austenite stability vary among steel grades.
